subject: chemistry
title: Organic Chemistry Adventure 1: Functional groups and homologous series
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet functional groups — alkanes to carboxylic acids.
meta_desc: Chemistry — functional groups, homologous series, IUPAC nomenclature.
final_note: You learned organic compounds form homologous series, each with characteristic functional group and reactions.

concepts.def: Compound of just C and H

walkthroughs.body_html:
IUPAC: pick longest chain, identify functional group → suffix; number to give lowest locant.

Examples:
- CH₃CH₂CH₃ = propane.
- CH₃CH=CH₂ = propene.
- CH₃CH₂OH = ethanol.
- CH₃COOH = ethanoic acid.
- CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ = 2-methylpropane.

Common groups + suffixes:

- Alkane (-ane): C-C, e.g. butane.
- Alkene (-ene): C=C, e.g. but-1-ene.
- Alcohol (-ol): -OH, e.g. butan-1-ol.
- Halogenoalkane: -F/Cl/Br/I.
- Aldehyde (-al): -CHO.
- Ketone (-one): C=O within chain.
- Carboxylic acid (-oic acid): -COOH.
- Ester (-oate): -COO-.
- Amine (-amine): -NH₂.

Structural isomers share molecular formula but differ in connection.

C₄H₁₀: butane and 2-methylpropane.
C₄H₈: but-1-ene, but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene, cyclobutane.

Stereoisomers — same atoms + bonds, different spatial arrangement.
- Cis-trans (E/Z) around C=C.
- Optical isomers (enantiomers) around chiral C.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.
Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.

mcqs.q: When HBr adds to propene, why does Br preferentially attach to the middle carbon?
options: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Br adds to whichever carbon has more hydrogens already.
Br always adds to the end carbon because it's the most accessible.
The more stable secondary carbocation forms preferentially as the intermediate, so Br adds there (Markovnikov's rule).
